claim: Genetically identical plants growing in the same conditions can display heterogeneous phenotypes.
source: Genetically identical plants growing in the same conditions can display heterogeneous phenotypes.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that sets up the study's context.

claim: Arabidopsis seed germination time is used as a model system to examine phenotypic variability and its underlying mechanisms.
source: Here we use Arabidopsis seed germination time as a model system to examine phenotypic variability and its underlying mechanisms.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the study's approach.

claim: There is extensive variation in seed germination time variability between Arabidopsis accessions.
source: We show extensive variation in seed germination time variability between Arabidopsis accessions and use a multiparent recombinant inbred population to identify two genetic loci involved in this trait.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Two genetic loci are involved in seed germination time variability.
source: We show extensive variation in seed germination time variability between Arabidopsis accessions and use a multiparent recombinant inbred population to identify two genetic loci involved in this trait.
evidence: This is based on QTL mapping results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both loci identified include genes implicated in modulating abscisic acid (ABA) sensitivity.
source: Both loci include genes implicated in modulating abscisic acid (ABA) sensitivity.
evidence: This is based on analysis of candidate genes at the identified QTL.

claim: Mutually antagonistic regulation between ABA and GA underlies the decision to germinate.
source: Mutually antagonistic regulation between ABA, which represses germination, and gibberellic acid (GA), which promotes germination, underlies the decision to germinate and can act as a bistable switch.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field and is cited in the manuscript.

claim: The ABA-GA network can act as a bistable switch.
source: Mutually antagonistic regulation between ABA, which represses germination, and gibberellic acid (GA), which promotes germination, underlies the decision to germinate and can act as a bistable switch.
evidence: This is supported by modeling and previous experimental work cited in the manuscript.

claim: A simple stochastic model of the ABA-GA network shows that modulating ABA sensitivity can generate the range of germination time distributions observed experimentally.
source: A simple stochastic model of the ABA-GA network shows that modulating ABA sensitivity can generate the range of germination time distributions we observe experimentally.
evidence: This is based on modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The model's predictions on the effects of exogenous hormone addition were validated experimentally.
source: We validate the model by testing its predictions on the effects of exogenous hormone addition.
evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing model predictions to experimental results.

claim: Exhibiting a range of phenotypes may promote species survival in an environment where current cues cannot predict future conditions.
source: In an environment where current cues cannot be used to predict future conditions, exhibiting a range of phenotypes may promote species survival.
evidence: This is based on theoretical considerations and cited literature.

claim: A population can hedge its bets against an uncertain environment by maintaining genetic variation within the population.
source: A population can hedge its bets against an uncertain environment by maintaining genetic variation within the population (e.g. balancing selection Delph and Kelly, 2014) or by containing a single genotype that produces a variety of phenotypes (a diversified bet-hedging strategy Cohen, 1966; Lewontin and Cohen, 1969; Philippi and Seger, 1989; Simons, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: A population can hedge its bets against an uncertain environment by containing a single genotype that produces a variety of phenotypes (a diversified bet-hedging strategy).
source: A population can hedge its bets against an uncertain environment by maintaining genetic variation within the population (e.g. balancing selection Delph and Kelly, 2014) or by containing a single genotype that produces a variety of phenotypes (a diversified bet-hedging strategy Cohen, 1966; Lewontin and Cohen, 1969; Philippi and Seger, 1989; Simons, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Bacteria can use diversified bet-hedging strategies to survive antibiotic treatments.
source: Bacteria can use diversified bet-hedging strategies to survive a range of changes of condition, including antibiotic treatments (Balaban et al., 2004; Martins and Locke, 2015) and other environmental stresses (Patange et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Bacteria can use diversified bet-hedging strategies to survive other environmental stresses.
source: Bacteria can use diversified bet-hedging strategies to survive a range of changes of condition, including antibiotic treatments (Balaban et al., 2004; Martins and Locke, 2015) and other environmental stresses (Patange et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Phenotypic variability among genetically identical individuals is generated by genetic networks amplifying stochasticity in molecular interactions.
source: Mechanistic studies suggest that the required phenotypic variability among genetically identical individuals is generated by genetic networks amplifying stochasticity in molecular interactions to generate a range of outputs (Alon, 2007; Eldar and Elowitz, 2010; Viney and Reece, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mechanistic studies.

claim: Theoretical work shows that variability in the germination time of genetically identical seeds is likely to be advantageous in environments that are unpredictable.
source: In plants, theoretical work shows that variability in the germination time of genetically identical seeds is likely to be advantageous in environments that are unpredictable (Cohen, 1966; Simons, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Ecological studies have found that variability in seed germination time is correlated with environmental unpredictability.
source: Indeed, ecological studies have found that variability in seed germination time is correlated with environmental unpredictability (Simons and Johnston, 2006; Venable, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to ecological studies.

claim: Seeds can enter a 'dormant' state, refractory to germination even under favourable germination conditions.
source: Seeds can enter a 'dormant' state, refractory to germination even under favourable germination conditions (Baskin and Baskin, 2004; Bewley, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on seed dormancy.

claim: Seed dormancy is a continuous variable, with genetically identical seeds having different depths of dormancy.
source: Seed dormancy is a continuous variable, with genetically identical seeds having different depths of dormancy (Finch-Savage and Leubner-Metzger, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on seed dormancy.

claim: The decision to germinate is controlled by the balance between gibberellic acid (GA), which promotes germination, and abscisic acid (ABA), which represses it.
source: In-depth molecular studies have shown that the decision to germinate is controlled by the balance between two hormones, gibberellic acid (GA), which promotes germination, and abscisic acid (ABA), which represses it (Liu and Hou, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review of molecular studies.

claim: ABA and GA function in a mutually antagonistic manner by each inhibiting the synthesis and promoting the degradation of the other.
source: These hormones function in a mutually antagonistic manner by each inhibiting the synthesis and promoting the degradation of the other (Liu and Hou, 2018; Piskurewicz et al., 2008; Topham et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to molecular studies.

claim: ABA and GA have opposing effects on downstream transcriptional regulators that control the balance between dormancy and germination.
source: Additionally, the two hormones have opposing effects on downstream transcriptional regulators that control the balance between dormancy and germination (Liu et al., 2016; Piskurewicz et al., 2008; Shu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to molecular studies.

claim: Variable germination times can be generated by variation in sensitivities to germination regulators in a batch of seeds.
source: Pioneering modelling work has suggested that variable germination times can be generated by variation in sensitivities to germination regulators in a batch of seeds (Bradford, 1990; Bradford and Trewavas, 1994) or due to stochastic fluctuations in the regulators of ABA (Johnston and Bassel, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to modeling work.

claim: Variable germination times can be generated due to stochastic fluctuations in the regulators of ABA.
source: Pioneering modelling work has suggested that variable germination times can be generated by variation in sensitivities to germination regulators in a batch of seeds (Bradford, 1990; Bradford and Trewavas, 1994) or due to stochastic fluctuations in the regulators of ABA (Johnston and Bassel, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to modeling work.

claim: The ABA-GA network can be described as a bistable switch due to the mutual inhibition between ABA and GA.
source: Interestingly, a combination of experiment and modelling has revealed that the ABA-GA network can be described as a bistable switch due to the mutual inhibition between ABA and GA, leading to two possible states, a dormant high ABA low GA state, or a germinating low ABA high GA state (Topham et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study combining experiment and modeling.

claim: The ABA-GA bistable switch leads to two possible states: a dormant high ABA low GA state, or a germinating low ABA high GA state.
source: Interestingly, a combination of experiment and modelling has revealed that the ABA-GA network can be described as a bistable switch due to the mutual inhibition between ABA and GA, leading to two possible states, a dormant high ABA low GA state, or a germinating low ABA high GA state (Topham et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study combining experiment and modeling.

claim: The ABA-GA bistable switch can explain the observation that Arabidopsis seed germination is more effectively triggered by fluctuating temperatures than continuous cold.
source: This regulatory motif can explain the observation that Arabidopsis seed germination is more effectively triggered by fluctuating temperatures than continuous cold (Topham et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study.

claim: The MAGIC lines exhibited transgressive segregation, with greater variation in CV than the parental accessions.
source: The MAGIC lines exhibited transgressive segregation, with greater variation in CV than the parental accessions (Figure 1A, compare orange and blue distributions, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: A small number of MAGIC lines (8 out of 341 characterised) had very high CVs of germination time (>0.6) compared to the rest.
source: A small number of MAGIC lines (8 out of 341 characterised) had very high CVs of germination time (>0.6) compared to the rest (Figure 1B), which was due to a fraction of seeds germinating very late, giving rise to bimodal distributions (e.g. M178 and M182 in Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Very high CVs in some MAGIC lines were due to a fraction of seeds germinating very late, giving rise to bimodal distributions.
source: A small number of MAGIC lines (8 out of 341 characterised) had very high CVs of germination time (>0.6) compared to the rest (Figure 1B), which was due to a fraction of seeds germinating very late, giving rise to bimodal distributions (e.g. M178 and M182 in Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The CV of most MAGIC lines tested was similar between repeat experiments involving independent seed harvests and sowing.
source: The CV of most MAGIC lines tested was similar between repeat experiments involving independent seed harvests and sowing (Figure 1C) (Pearson's r = 0.88, 95% CI [0.76, 0.94] for all lines for which repeats were done).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1C and statistical analysis.

claim: CVs for the MAGIC parental lines remained similar over a range of lengths of dry storage period (30–60 days of dry storage).
source: We confirmed that CVs for the MAGIC parental lines remained similar over a range of lengths of dry storage period (30–60 days of dry storage), demonstrating that our results are not specific to one condition (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The broad-sense heritability for CV was estimated to be ~40%.
source: The broad-sense heritability (defined as the ratio of total genetic variance to total phenotypic variance) for CV was estimated to be ~40%, which is at the upper limit of heritabilities previously measured for variability in a number of post-germination plant traits (Hall et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the experimental data and comparison to cited literature.

claim: For high variability lines tested, the full range of germination times observed in whole-plant samples was also present in seed from individual siliques.
source: For these lines, the full range of germination times observed in whole-plant samples was also present in seed from individual siliques (Figure 2A, B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Variability in seed germination time can arise independently of position or age differences between siliques.
source: This suggests that variability in seed germination time can arise independently of position or age differences between siliques.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing variability within single siliques.

claim: For the lines tested, late and early germinating seeds were produced by both halves of the siliques, with no consistent differences between the top and bottom halves of siliques in the fraction of seeds that germinated late.
source: For the lines tested, late and early germinating seeds were produced by both halves of the siliques, with no consistent differences between the top and bottom halves of siliques in the fraction of seeds that germinated late (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B,D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Variability in germination time in the lines tested can arise independently of positional or maturation gradients within the whole plant or individual siliques.
source: Thus, variability in germination time in the lines tested can arise independently of positional or maturation gradients within the whole plant or individual siliques.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing no consistent differences between silique halves.

claim: A mechanism exists to generate differences in germination behaviour of equivalent seeds from the same silique, which is not dependent on gradients of regulatory molecules along the fruit.
source: This suggests that a mechanism exists to generate differences in germination behaviour of equivalent seeds from the same silique, which is not dependent on gradients of regulatory molecules along the fruit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: There are weak correlations between CV and mode or percentage germination in the MAGIC lines.
source: We found weak correlations between CV and mode or percentage germination, with lower variability lines (low CV) tending to have a lower mode days to germination and higher percentage germination (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Lower variability lines (low CV) tend to have a lower mode days to germination and higher percentage germination.
source: We found weak correlations between CV and mode or percentage germination, with lower variability lines (low CV) tending to have a lower mode days to germination and higher percentage germination (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Within the MAGIC population, variability is correlated with percentage germination and modal germination time, but can be uncoupled from these traits.
source: Thus, within the MAGIC population, variability is correlated with percentage germination and modal germination time, but can be uncoupled from these traits.
evidence: This is based on experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: QTL mapping for the full set of lines and the set excluding bimodal lines revealed a region of chromosome 3 (i.e. Chr3) that accounted for ~14% of the variance in CV of germination time in the MAGIC lines used.
source: QTL mapping for both the full set of lines and the set excluding bimodal lines revealed a region of chromosome 3 (i.e. Chr3) that accounted for ~14% of the variance in CV of germination time in the MAGIC lines used (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is based on QTL mapping results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The tip of the Chr3 QTL peak co-located with the previously identified DELAY OF GERMINATION 6 (DOG6) QTL, at 15.9 Mb.
source: The tip of the peak co-located with the previously identified DELAY OF GERMINATION 6 (DOG6) QTL, at 15.9 Mb (Bentsink et al., 2010; Hanzi, 2014).
evidence: This is based on QTL mapping results and comparison to previously published QTL.

claim: The Chr3 QTL was also associated with mean days to germination, mode days to germination and percentage germination.
source: This Chr3 QTL was also associated with mean days to germination, mode days to germination and percentage germination, suggesting that this locus is a general regulator of germination time, rather than specifically affecting variability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on QTL mapping results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Chr3 QTL is a general regulator of germination time, rather than specifically affecting variability.
source: This Chr3 QTL was also associated with mean days to germination, mode days to germination and percentage germination, suggesting that this locus is a general regulator of germination time, rather than specifically affecting variability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the QTL mapping results.

claim: A putative QTL at 19.8 Mb on chromosome 5 (i.e., Chr5) was revealed to be associated with CV when the Chr3 QTL genotype was used as a covariate in the model.
source: This revealed a further putative QTL at 19.8 Mb on chromosome 5 (i.e., Chr5) associated with CV (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on QTL mapping results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Chr5 QTL was not significantly associated with mode or mean days to germination or percentage germination.
source: Unlike the Chr3 locus, this one was not significantly associated with mode or mean days to germination or percentage germination (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on QTL mapping results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Chr5 QTL accounts for an extra 9% of the variance in CV of the MAGIC lines used.
source: This locus accounts for an extra 9% of the variance in CV of the MAGIC lines used.
evidence: This is based on QTL mapping results.

claim: The Chr5 QTL peak lies ~1.2 Mb downstream of the DELAY OF GERMINATION 1 (DOG1, AT5G45830 ) gene (at 18.59 Mb) and ~1.2 Mb upstream from the SEEDLING EMERGENCE TIME 1 (SET1) locus (at ~21 Mb).
source: The QTL peak lies ~1.2 Mb downstream of the DELAY OF GERMINATION 1 (DOG1, AT5G45830 ) gene (at 18.59 Mb) and ~1.2 Mb upstream from the SEEDLING EMERGENCE TIME 1 (SET1) locus (at ~21 Mb) (Footitt et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on QTL mapping results and comparison to known gene locations.

claim: For the Chr3 QTL, there was a relatively strong negative correlation between haplotypic effects on CV and percentage germination, and a positive correlation between effects on CV and mode.
source: For the Chr3 QTL, there was a relatively strong negative correlation between haplotypic effects on CV and percentage germination, and a positive correlation between effects on CV and mode (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of QTL effects shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: For the Chr5 QTL, there was a negative correlation between haplotypic effects on CV and percentage germination, but there was no correlation between their effects on CV and on mode.
source: For the Chr5 QTL, there was a negative correlation between haplotypic effects on CV and percentage germination, but there was no correlation between their effects on CV and on mode (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of QTL effects shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Bulk-segregant analysis using whole-genome pooled sequencing of F2 pools from a Col-0 × No-0 cross independently verified that a locus at ~20 Mb of Chr5 has an influence on variability.
source: The results independently verified that a locus at ~20 Mb of Chr5 has an influence on variability.
evidence: This is based on bulk-segregant analysis results.

claim: In the bulk-segregant analysis, the peak of association was located at 18.6 Mb on Chr5, which overlaps precisely with the DOG1 gene.
source: In this experiment, the peak of association was located at 18.6 Mb on Chr5, which overlaps precisely with the DOG1 gene (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on bulk-segregant analysis results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Late germinating F2 plants produced seeds with higher CVs of germination time, lower percentages of germination and similar average germination times compared to seeds of early germinating F2 plants.
source: This showed that late germinating F2 plants produced seeds with higher CVs of germination time, lower percentages of germination and similar average germination times compared to seeds of early germinating F2 plants (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: At least two loci contribute to variability in seed germination time in the MAGIC lines (Chr3, ~16 Mb and Chr5, ~18.6/19.8 Mb).
source: In summary, we have shown that at least two loci contribute to variability in seed germination time in the MAGIC lines (Chr3, ~16 Mb and Chr5, ~18.6/19.8 Mb).
evidence: This is a summary of the QTL mapping results.

claim: The best candidate genes underlying the identified loci influence ABA sensitivity.
source: There is evidence to suggest that the best candidate genes underlying our identified loci influence ABA sensitivity.
evidence: This is based on analysis of candidate genes and their known functions.

claim: The effect of the DOG6 locus overlapping the Chr3 QTL is proposed to be caused by the ANAC060 gene.
source: The effect of the DOG6 locus overlapping our Chr3 QTL is proposed to be caused by the ANAC060 gene (Hanzi, 2014), which influences ABA sensitivity in seedlings, directly binds to the promoter of the ABA-responsive transcription factor, ABA INSENSITIVE 5 (ABI5), and can downregulate expression of both ABI4 and ABI5 (Li et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on citations to published studies.

claim: ANAC060 influences ABA sensitivity in seedlings, directly binds to the promoter of ABI5, and can downregulate expression of both ABI4 and ABI5.
source: The effect of the DOG6 locus overlapping our Chr3 QTL is proposed to be caused by the ANAC060 gene (Hanzi, 2014), which influences ABA sensitivity in seedlings, directly binds to the promoter of the ABA-responsive transcription factor, ABA INSENSITIVE 5 (ABI5), and can downregulate expression of both ABI4 and ABI5 (Li et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on citations to published studies.

claim: The SET1 locus in the Chr5 region is hypothesised to be caused by the ABA‐HYPERSENSITIVE GERMINATION 1 (AHG1) gene.
source: The SET1 locus in this region is hypothesised to be caused by the ABA‐HYPERSENSITIVE GERMINATION 1 (AHG1) gene (Footitt et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a published study.

claim: AHG1 is a type 2C protein phosphatase (PP2C) that inhibits ABA signalling via dephosphorylating class II SNF1-related protein kinase 2 (SnRK2), which promote seed dormancy by activating ABA-responsive transcriptional changes.
source: AHG1 is a type 2C protein phosphatase (PP2C) that inhibits ABA signalling via dephosphorylating class II SNF1-related protein kinase 2 (SnRK2), which promote seed dormancy by activating ABA-responsive transcriptional changes (Liu and Hou, 2018; Née et al., 2017a; Nishimura et al., 2007, Nishimura et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on citations to published studies.

claim: DOG1 has been shown to directly bind to AHG1, independently from ABA, and inhibit its function, thus allowing DOG1 to inhibit germination via the ABA pathway.
source: DOG1 has been shown to directly bind to AHG1, independently from ABA, and inhibit its function, thus allowing DOG1 to inhibit germination via the ABA pathway (Carrillo-Barral et al., 2020; Née et al., 2017a; Nishimura et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on citations to published studies.

claim: anac060 mutant seedlings and ahg1 mutant seeds have increased ABA sensitivity.
source: Mutants of all three candidate genes have altered ABA sensitivity: anac060 mutant seedlings and ahg1 mutant seeds have increased ABA sensitivity (Yu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2014; Nishimura et al., 2007), while dog1 mutant seeds have decreased ABA sensitivity (Née et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is based on citations to published studies.

claim: dog1 mutant seeds have decreased ABA sensitivity.
source: Mutants of all three candidate genes have altered ABA sensitivity: anac060 mutant seedlings and ahg1 mutant seeds have increased ABA sensitivity (Yu et al., 2020; Li et al., 2014; Nishimura et al., 2007), while dog1 mutant seeds have decreased ABA sensitivity (Née et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is based on citations to published studies.

claim: The dog1-3 mutant in the Col-0 background consistently had reduced CV of germination time, and reduced mean and mode days to germination compared to the wild type.
source: We tested these mutants for their effects on germination time distributions and found that the dog1-3 mutant in the Col-0 background (Bentsink et al., 2006) consistently had reduced CV of germination time, and reduced mean and mode days to germination compared to the wild type (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A.

claim: The dog1 mutant in the No-0 background showed a similar phenotype to dog1-3 in Col-0, with reduced CV, mean and mode.
source: The dog1 mutant in the No-0 background showed a similar phenotype to dog1-3 in Col-0, with reduced CV, mean and mode (Figure 4—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5C.

claim: Reduced ABA sensitivity of the dog1 mutants in the Col-0 and No-0 backgrounds was observed in germination assays, with higher levels of exogenous ABA required to observe a change in the germination fraction.
source: Consistent with previously published work (Née et al., 2017a), we observed reduced ABA sensitivity of the dog1 mutants in the Col-0 and No-0 backgrounds in our germination assays, with higher levels of exogenous ABA required to observe a change in the germination fraction (Figure 4—figure supplement 5B, D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5B, D and comparison to published work.

claim: The ahg1-5 mutant in the Col-0 background showed a slight increase in CV of germination time, which was associated with an increase in ABA sensitivity.
source: On the other hand, the ahg1-5 mutant in the Col-0 background (Née et al., 2017a) showed a slight increase in CV of germination time, which was associated with an increase in ABA sensitivity (Figure 4—figure supplement 5E, F).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5E, F.

claim: Both DOG1 and AHG1 candidate genes for the Chr5 locus have an effect on the CV of germination time which is consistent with their altered ABA sensitivities.
source: Thus, both of these candidate genes for the Chr5 locus have an effect on the CV of germination time which is consistent with their altered ABA sensitivities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data on mutants.

claim: For the anac060 mutant in the Col-0 background, a slight increase in CV was observed, with an increase in mode and decrease in percentage germination compared to Col-0 in seed sown 3 DAH.
source: For the anac060 mutant in the Col-0 background (Li et al., 2014), we observed a slight increase in CV, with an increase in mode and decrease in percentage germination compared to Col-0 in seed sown 3 DAH (Figure 4—figure supplement 5G, 3 DAH), but did not see a convincing phenotype in seeds that were stored for 30 days prior to sowing (i.e. in the same conditions as the MAGIC lines used for QTL mapping) (Figure 4—figure supplement 5G, 30 DAH).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5G.

claim: A convincing phenotype for the anac060 mutant was not seen in seeds that were stored for 30 days prior to sowing.
source: For the anac060 mutant in the Col-0 background (Li et al., 2014), we observed a slight increase in CV, with an increase in mode and decrease in percentage germination compared to Col-0 in seed sown 3 DAH (Figure 4—figure supplement 5G, 3 DAH), but did not see a convincing phenotype in seeds that were stored for 30 days prior to sowing (i.e. in the same conditions as the MAGIC lines used for QTL mapping) (Figure 4—figure supplement 5G, 30 DAH).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5G.

claim: A weak tendency towards an increase in ABA sensitivity in the anac060 mutant was observed, but this was not as striking as that reported in seedlings.
source: We observed a weak tendency towards an increase in ABA sensitivity in the anac060 mutant, but this was not as striking as that reported in seedlings (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on experimental data and comparison to published work.

claim: The candidate genes underlying the Chr5 QTL peak could influence variability through an effect on ABA sensitivity.
source: Overall, our results support the hypothesis that the candidate genes underlying the Chr5 QTL peak could influence variability through an effect on ABA sensitivity and suggest that this could also be the case for the ANAC060 candidate gene for the Chr3 QTL peak.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data on mutants.

claim: The ANAC060 candidate gene for the Chr3 QTL peak could influence variability through an effect on ABA sensitivity.
source: Overall, our results support the hypothesis that the candidate genes underlying the Chr5 QTL peak could influence variability through an effect on ABA sensitivity and suggest that this could also be the case for the ANAC060 candidate gene for the Chr3 QTL peak.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data on mutants.

claim: A simplified mathematical model of the core ABA-GA network that governs germination time was built.
source: To answer this, we built a simplified mathematical model of the core ABA-GA network that governs germination time (Liu and Hou, 2018; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach.

claim: The model includes both ABA and GA since the decision to germinate is governed by the relative levels of the two hormones.
source: We reasoned that it was necessary to include both ABA and GA in the model since the decision to germinate is governed by the relative levels of the two hormones (Née et al., 2017b; Shu et al., 2016b), and both converge to regulate the expression of a common set of transcription factors that control seed dormancy and germination (Liu and Hou, 2018; Piskurewicz et al., 2008; Shu et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is a justification for the model structure based on cited literature.

claim: The model represents the inhibitors of germination – DELLAs, ABI4 and ABI5 – as one factor, called Integrator.
source: We represent the inhibitors of germination – DELLAs, ABI4 and ABI5 – as one factor, called Integrator, which we assume must drop below a threshold for germination to occur.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: The model assumes that Integrator must drop below a threshold for germination to occur.
source: We represent the inhibitors of germination – DELLAs, ABI4 and ABI5 – as one factor, called Integrator, which we assume must drop below a threshold for germination to occur.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: The model assumes that ABA promotes the production of Integrator and that GA promotes its degradation.
source: We assume that ABA promotes the production of Integrator and that GA promotes its degradation.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: The model assumes that Integrator promotes ABA production and inhibits GA production.
source: Integrator is assumed to promote ABA production and inhibit GA production.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: The model includes a factor, Z, that increases upon sowing and promotes GA production.
source: A factor, Z, increases upon sowing and promotes GA production.
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: Modulating ABA sensitivity can generate the range of germination time distributions observed experimentally.
source: A simple stochastic model of the ABA-GA network shows that modulating ABA sensitivity can generate the range of germination time distributions we observe experimentally.
evidence: This is based on modeling results.

claim: Varying the parameter governing the ABA threshold for Integrator production can cause correlated effects on CV and mode.
source: To investigate the effect of ABA sensitivity on germination time distributions in the model, we varied the parameter governing the ABA threshold for Integrator production, which is inversely correlated with the sensitivity to ABA (see Materials and methods). Varying this parameter can cause correlated effects on CV and mode (Figure 5B) and can account for a range of germination time distributions, from less variable (i.e. more peaked), to more variable (i.e. long tailed) (Figure 5C), that qualitatively match the range of germination time distributions we observe experimentally (Figure 1A, Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Varying the ABA threshold for Integrator production parameter can account for a range of germination time distributions, from less variable to more variable, that qualitatively match the range observed experimentally.
source: To investigate the effect of ABA sensitivity on germination time distributions in the model, we varied the parameter governing the ABA threshold for Integrator production, which is inversely correlated with the sensitivity to ABA (see Materials and methods). Varying this parameter can cause correlated effects on CV and mode (Figure 5B) and can account for a range of germination time distributions, from less variable (i.e. more peaked), to more variable (i.e. long tailed) (Figure 5C), that qualitatively match the range of germination time distributions we observe experimentally (Figure 1A, Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: As the sensitivity of integrator to ABA increases, the germination time distributions are more long tailed with a higher CV and mode.
source: As the sensitivity of integrator to ABA increases (lower values of ABA threshold for integrator production), the germination time distributions are more long tailed with a higher CV and mode (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: With low sensitivity to ABA, the model is monostable after sowing, with the high GA, low ABA, low Integrator (germination) steady state the only stable state after the sowing-induced rise in GA production.
source: With low sensitivity to ABA, the model is monostable after sowing, with the high GA, low ABA, low Integrator (germination) steady state the only stable state after the sowing-induced rise in GA production (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: With higher ABA sensitivity, the model is bistable after sowing and the rise in GA production, with a low GA, high ABA, high integrator (non-germination) steady state in addition to the germination steady state both existing after sowing.
source: With higher ABA sensitivity, the model is bistable after sowing and the rise in GA production, with a low GA, high ABA, high integrator (non-germination) steady state in addition to the germination steady state both existing after sowing (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H, I).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the bistable scenario, after the rise in GA production, seeds can remain in the non-germination steady state for some time but are driven to transition to the germination steady state by stochastic fluctuations, which results in variable germination times and a later average germination time.
source: In this bistable scenario, after the rise in GA production, seeds can remain in the non-germination steady state for some time but are driven to transition to the germination steady state by stochastic fluctuations, which results in variable germination times and a later average germination time (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–N).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The bistable regime is associated with an increase in CV and mode of germination time.
source: Hence, the bistable regime is associated with an increase in CV and mode of germination time (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The coupled variation in CV and mode of MAGIC line germination time distributions can be at least partly accounted for by variation in the parameter controlling the sensitivity of integrator production to ABA.
source: Thus, the coupled variation in CV and mode of MAGIC line germination time distributions can be at least partly accounted for by variation in the parameter controlling the sensitivity of integrator production to ABA: as the sensitivity to ABA increases, the model becomes bistable, with later and more variable germination times.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results.

claim: Once within the bistable regime, increases in ABA sensitivity increase the stability of the non-germination steady state.
source: Additionally, once within the bistable regime, increases in ABA sensitivity increase the stability of the non-germination steady state (Figure 5—figure supplement 1O–U compared with Figure 5—figure supplement 1H–N).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increases in the stability of the non-germination steady state can result in an increasing proportion of seeds remaining in this state and not germinating (decreasing percentage germination) and can also further increase the variability of germination time of the seeds that do germinate.
source: This can result in an increasing proportion of seeds remaining in this state and not germinating (decreasing percentage germination) and can also further increase the variability of germination time of the seeds that do germinate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1Q–U compared to Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–N).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Natural variation between MAGIC lines in the variability of germination time could be due to differences in ABA sensitivity that cause the ABA-GA network to operate in different regimes (i.e. monostable versus bistable) in different lines.
source: Hence, we hypothesise that natural variation between MAGIC lines in the variability of germination time could be due to differences in ABA sensitivity that cause (i) the ABA-GA network to operate in different regimes (i.e. monostable versus bistable) in different lines and (ii) differences between lines in the stability of the non-germination steady state.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the modeling results.

claim: Natural variation between MAGIC lines in the variability of germination time could be due to differences in ABA sensitivity that cause differences between lines in the stability of the non-germination steady state.
source: Hence, we hypothesise that natural variation between MAGIC lines in the variability of germination time could be due to differences in ABA sensitivity that cause (i) the ABA-GA network to operate in different regimes (i.e. monostable versus bistable) in different lines and (ii) differences between lines in the stability of the non-germination steady state.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the modeling results.

claim: The model can capture multiple possible relationships between the CV and mode of germination time distributions, with the nature of the relationship changing depending on which parameter was being varied.
source: We found that the model could capture multiple possible relationships between the CV and mode of germination time distributions, with the nature of the relationship changing depending on which parameter was being varied.
evidence: This is based on modeling results from parameter screens.

claim: A number of parameters showed positively correlated effects on CV and mode.
source: A number of parameters showed positively correlated effects on CV and mode (e.g. Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), although the strength of this correlation varied depending on the region of parameter space and the parameter being changed (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and 4.

claim: Positive correlations between effects on CV and mode were observed for parameters controlling the rates of basal production and degradation of GA, ABA and Integrator as well as for those controlling the GA-dependent degradation rate of the Integrator.
source: Positive correlations between the effects on CV and mode were also observed for the sensitivity of ABA production to Integrator levels (we define sensitivity as the inverse of the Integrator threshold for promotion of ABA production and use the equivalent definition for all subsequent sensitivity parameters; see Figure 5—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Multiple other parameters in addition to that governing ABA sensitivity could account for the positive correlation between CV and mode of germination time distributions in the MAGIC lines.
source: Thus, multiple other parameters in addition to that governing ABA sensitivity (Figure 5B, C, Figure 5—figure supplement 4F, G) could account for the positive correlation between CV and mode of germination time distributions in the MAGIC lines.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results.

claim: In most cases, low percentage germination tends to be associated with high CV and mode while high percentage germination tends to be associated with low CV and mode.
source: In most cases, low percentage germination tends to be associated with high CV and mode while high percentage germination tends to be associated with low CV and mode, similar to the correlations observed within the MAGIC lines (e.g. see Figure 5B, C, Figure 5—figure supplement 4A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on modeling results and comparison to experimental data.

claim: Some parameters showed both correlated and anti-correlated effects on CV and mode and some generated decoupled changes in CV and mode.
source: For example, for the parameter controlling basal GA production and that controlling the rate of Integrator production, in addition to the positively correlated effects on CV and mode described above, anti-correlated effects on these traits were also observed in other regions in parameter space (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B, C).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: For some areas of parameter space, anti-correlated effects on CV and mode occurred when modulating the sensitivity of the Integrator to GA-promoted degradation.
source: For some areas of parameter space, anti-correlated effects on CV and mode occurred when modulating the sensitivity of the Integrator to GA-promoted degradation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, Figure 5—figure supplement 3B, Figure 5—figure supplement 4F, H).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2, 3, and 4.

claim: Somewhat decoupled changes in CV and mode were observed when varying the parameter that controls the level of noise in the system, such that, for some regions of parameter space, reductions in noise decreased the CV while maintaining a relatively constant mode and percentage germination.
source: Somewhat decoupled changes in CV and mode were also observed when varying the parameter that controls the level of noise in the system, such that, for some regions of parameter space, reductions in noise decreased the CV while maintaining a relatively constant mode and percentage germination (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D, Figure 5—figure supplement 3D, Figure 5—figure supplement 4G, H).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2, 3, and 4.

claim: Across a range of parameter sets, both modes and CVs of germination times tend to be higher when bistability rather than monostability occurs after the sowing-induced rise in GA production.
source: We found that across a range of parameter sets, both modes and CVs of germination times tend to be higher when bistability rather than monostability occurs after the sowing-induced rise in GA production (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: The model predicts that high variability in germination time is associated with the ABA-GA network operating in the bistable regime.
source: Thus, in general, the model predicts that high variability in germination time is associated with the ABA-GA network operating in the bistable regime.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results.

claim: The model predicts that starting from germination time distributions with low or high variability, increasing concentrations of exogenous ABA will initially increase the CVs of the germination time distributions.
source: The model predicts that starting from germination time distributions with low or high variability, increasing concentrations of exogenous ABA will initially increase the CVs of the germination time distributions (Figure 6Ai), causing long-tailed distributions to emerge (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The addition of exogenous ABA stabilises the high Integrator, high ABA, low GA non-germination state, requiring stronger fluctuations to allow germination.
source: This is because the addition of exogenous ABA stabilises the high Integrator, high ABA, low GA non-germination state, requiring stronger fluctuations to allow germination (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: At higher concentrations of exogenous ABA, the germination time distribution becomes flattened into a seemingly uniform distribution with a high mean and therefore lower CV.
source: At higher concentrations of exogenous ABA, the germination time distribution becomes flattened into a seemingly uniform distribution with a high mean and therefore lower CV (Figure 6Ai, ii, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, [ABA]exo = 2.5).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The increase of exogenous ABA also reduces the percentage of germinated seeds.
source: Hence, the increase of exogenous ABA also reduces the percentage of germinated seeds (Figure 6Aiv).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 6Aiv.

claim: ABA treatments tended to increase the spread of germination time distributions, particularly for low variability lines.
source: ABA treatments tended to increase the spread of germination time distributions, particularly for low variability lines.
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: In the low variability lines, high ABA concentrations of 5 and 10 μM caused large increases in the CV of germination time, such that the distributions of germination times for low variability lines treated with ABA were similar to those of high variability lines in control conditions.
source: In the low variability lines, high ABA concentrations of 5 and 10 μM caused large increases in the CV of germination time, such that the distributions of germination times for low variability lines treated with ABA were similar to those of high variability lines in control conditions (Figure 6Bi, Figure 6—figure supplement 4A, compare Col-0, 5 and 10 μM [ABA]exo with M182, 0 μM [ABA]exo).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The experimental observation that the moderate ABA dose of 5 μM caused larger increases in CV compared with the changes in the mode was consistent with the model.
source: The experimental observation that the moderate ABA dose of 5 μM caused larger increases in CV compared with the changes in the mode was also consistent with the model (Figure 6Ai, iii, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, [ABA]exo = 0 compared to [ABA]exo = 1.5).
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data to modeling results.

claim: For high variability lines, increasing concentrations of ABA increased mean and mode germination times, but had relatively little effect on CV.
source: For high variability lines, increasing concentrations of ABA increased mean and mode germination times, but had relatively little effect on CV (Figure 6Bi-iii, Figure 6—figure supplement 4A, M182).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Consistent with a less striking effect of exogenous ABA on the CV of high variability lines compared to low variability lines, in the model, the fold changes in CV upon ABA addition for high variability lines were smaller than those predicted for low variability lines.
source: Consistent with a less striking effect of exogenous ABA on the CV of high variability lines compared to low variability lines, in the model, the fold changes in CV upon ABA addition for high variability lines were smaller than those predicted for low variability lines (Figure 6Ai).
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data to modeling results.

claim: Addition of exogenous GA to high and low variability lines in the simulations led to a reduced mode and less variable germination times.
source: In contrast to ABA treatments, addition of exogenous GA to high and low variability lines in the simulations led to a reduced mode and less variable germination times (Figure 6—figure supplement 1Ai, iii, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Addition of GA can destabilise and even destroy the high Integrator, high ABA and low GA non-germination steady state.
source: This is because addition of GA can destabilise and even destroy the high Integrator, high ABA and low GA non-germination steady state (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B), causing the model to become monostable.
evidence: This is based on modeling results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: When added experimentally to high and low variability MAGIC lines, GA tended to decrease the level of variability in germination time, with the effect strongest for the high variability genotypes.
source: As predicted by the model, when added experimentally to high and low variability MAGIC lines, GA tended to decrease the level of variability in germination time, with the effect strongest for the high variability genotypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, Figure 6—figure supplement 4B, M182).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and comparison to model predictions.

claim: High GA addition increased germination percentages and tended to decrease the mean germination time in high variability lines.
source: As expected from previous studies (Bewley, 1997; Koornneef and Karssen, 1994; Ni and Bradford, 1993), high GA addition also increased germination percentages and tended to decrease the mean germination time in high variability lines (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and comparison to previous studies.

claim: For low variability lines, GA had little effect on the variability (CV), percentage germination, mean or mode germination times.
source: For low variability lines, GA had little effect on the variability (CV), percentage germination, mean or mode germination times (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, Figure 6—figure supplement 4B, Col-0) as these lines germinated in a less variable manner with high percentage germination even in the absence of GA.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: For both ABA and GA, the overall effects of exogenous addition were qualitatively similar between the model and experiments.
source: Thus, for both ABA and GA, the overall effects of exogenous addition were qualitatively similar between the model and experiments.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data to modeling results.

claim: Loss of function of the CYP707A1 enzyme caused the Col-0 germination time distribution to become more long-tailed, with a small shift in the mode days to germination of ~1 day.
source: Similar to the effect of exogenous addition of ABA on low variability lines, loss of function of the CYP707A1 enzyme caused the Col-0 germination time distribution to become more long-tailed, with a small shift in the mode days to germination of ~1 day (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Loss of both CYP707A1 and CYP707A2 enzymes severely inhibited germination time and caused a large increase in the mode days to germination, similar to the effect of higher concentrations of exogenous ABA.
source: Loss of both enzymes severely inhibited germination time and caused a large increase in the mode days to germination, similar to the effect of higher concentrations of exogenous ABA, which in both cases is related to the germination time distribution becoming more uniform (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The correlated effect found on CV, mode and percentage germination due to a change in the ABA degradation rate is consistent with the results from changing the ABA degradation parameter in the model.
source: The correlated effect we found on CV, mode and percentage germination due to a change in the ABA degradation rate is also consistent with the results from changing the ABA degradation parameter in the model (Figure 5—figure supplement 4Ai-iii).
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data to modeling results.

claim: The ga3ox1-3 ga3ox2-1 mutant, which has reduced GA levels, showed an increased CV and, similar to the cyp707a1-1 cyp707a2-1 mutant, had increased mode and decreased percentage germination.
source: To test genetically the effect of decreasing the GA concentration on the germination time distribution of Col-0, we used the ga3ox1-3 ga3ox2-1 mutant, which lacks two enzymes involved in GA biosynthesis (Mitchum et al., 2006). This double mutant, which has reduced GA levels (Mitchum et al., 2006), showed an increased CV and, similar to the cyp707a1-1 cyp707a2-1 mutant, had increased mode and decreased percentage germination (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7 and comparison to cited literature.

claim: The findings on GA and ABA dose–response experiments and mutants support the model predictions regarding the effects of altering ABA and GA levels on CV, mode and percentage germination.
source: Together with the GA and ABA dose–response experiments, these findings support the model predictions regarding the effects of altering ABA and GA levels on CV, mode and percentage germination.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data to modeling results.

claim: Variability in seed germination time is relevant for plant survival in the wild, where high variability may function as a bet-hedging strategy.
source: Variability in seed germination time is relevant for plant survival in the wild, where high variability may function as a bet-hedging strategy.
evidence: This is based on theoretical considerations and cited literature.

claim: The advantages of variability in the wild contrast to the situation in agriculture, where minimal levels of variability are desirable to promote crop uniformity needed for optimal harvests.
source: The advantages of variability in the wild contrast to the situation in agriculture, where minimal levels of variability are desirable to promote crop uniformity needed for optimal harvests (Finch-Savage and Bassel, 2016; Mitchell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on citations to literature on agriculture.

claim: Germination time distributions are genetically controlled since they can vary greatly between different lines and are reproducible for a given genotype.
source: By describing detailed distributions of germination time for hundreds of Arabidopsis lines grown in a common environment, our work reveals that these distributions are genetically controlled since they can vary greatly between different lines and are reproducible for a given genotype.
evidence: This is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Candidate genes underlying the loci identified may alter germination time through influencing ABA sensitivity.
source: Using this natural variation, we identified two loci underlying variability and present evidence that candidate genes underlying the loci may alter germination time through influencing ABA sensitivity.
evidence: This is based on QTL mapping and analysis of candidate genes.

claim: Modelling and experiments show that perturbation of the ABA-GA network can modulate variability in germination times in a predictable manner.
source: Furthermore, modelling and experiments show that perturbation of the ABA-GA network can modulate variability in germination times in a predictable manner.
evidence: This is based on modeling and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: High or low variability could be specifically selected for both in the wild and in crop breeding programmes.
source: These findings suggest that high or low variability could be specifically selected for both in the wild and in crop breeding programmes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: In some Arabidopsis accessions, seeds matured on primary inflorescences had different germination behaviours to those that developed on branches.
source: Previously it was shown that, in some Arabidopsis accessions, seeds matured on primary inflorescences had different germination behaviours to those that developed on branches (Boyd et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a published study.

claim: Developmental differences exist along the Arabidopsis inflorescence, and these developmental differences between flowers could, in principle, create differences in seed germination time between fruits.
source: It was also reported that developmental differences exist along the Arabidopsis inflorescence, and these developmental differences between flowers could, in principle, create differences in seed germination time between fruits (Plackett et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a published study.

claim: Variability in germination time exists even for seeds from the same silique of Arabidopsis, suggesting that it can arise independently from developmental gradients in the plant.
source: Here we show that variability in germination time exists even for seeds from the same silique of Arabidopsis, suggesting that it can arise independently from developmental gradients in the plant.
evidence: This is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Seeds from proximal and distal halves of siliques have similar germination behaviours, indicating that variability is likely not caused by gradients of regulatory molecules along the length of the fruit.
source: We also show that seeds from proximal and distal halves of siliques have similar germination behaviours, indicating that variability is likely not caused by gradients of regulatory molecules along the length of the fruit.
evidence: This is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Chr3 and Chr5 QTL together only account for 23% of the variance in CV in the MAGIC lines.
source: Since it is likely that we have not detected all genetic loci that influence germination time distributions in our QTL mapping (the Chr3 and Chr5 QTL together only account for 23% of the variance in CV in the MAGIC lines), it is possible that undetected genetic variation in multiple components of the ABA-GA network contributes to the variation in germination time distributions that we observe and the complex relationship between CV, mode and percentage germination in the data.
evidence: This is based on QTL mapping results.

claim: Undetected genetic variation in multiple components of the ABA-GA network may contribute to the variation in germination time distributions observed and the complex relationship between CV, mode and percentage germination in the data.
source: Since it is likely that we have not detected all genetic loci that influence germination time distributions in our QTL mapping (the Chr3 and Chr5 QTL together only account for 23% of the variance in CV in the MAGIC lines), it is possible that undetected genetic variation in multiple components of the ABA-GA network contributes to the variation in germination time distributions that we observe and the complex relationship between CV, mode and percentage germination in the data.
evidence: This is an inference based on the QTL mapping results and modeling.

claim: The model behaves as a time-dependent toggle switch with stochastic fluctuations.
source: Because germination in our model is driven by the rise in GA production that occurs upon sowing, it behaves as a time-dependent toggle switch (Verd et al., 2014) with stochastic fluctuations.
evidence: This is a description of the model behavior.

claim: A time-dependent toggle switch with stochastic fluctuations can be used as a framework to understand variable germination behaviour.
source: Thus, our work shows that a time-dependent toggle switch (Verd et al., 2014) with stochastic fluctuations can be used as a framework to understand variable germination behaviour.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results.

claim: Feedback acting upon ABA biosynthesis and catabolism can modulate variability in ABA concentrations independent of the mean concentration.
source: Recent work has shown that feedback acting upon ABA biosynthesis and catabolism can modulate variability in ABA concentrations independent of the mean concentration (Johnston and Bassel, 2018).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a published study.

claim: The decision to germinate is likely made by groups of cells in the embryonic root.
source: In fact, the decision to germinate is likely made by groups of cells in the embryonic root (Mitchell et al., 2020; Topham et al., 2017), and thus it is unclear how the noise arising in individual cellular compartments would influence this multicellular decision.
evidence: This is based on citations to published studies.

claim: Noise in gene expression and phenotypic outputs has been reported for multiple pathways in plants.
source: On the other hand, noise in gene expression and phenotypic outputs has been reported for multiple pathways in plants (Jimenez-Gomez et al., 2011; Joseph et al., 2015), and recent work quantifying genome-wide transcriptional variability among individual seedlings in the same environment shows that, for many genes, there is a large degree of between-plant variability in transcript levels (Cortijo et al., 2019), suggesting that variability is not always averaged out to give uniformity of multicellular individuals.
evidence: This is based on citations to published studies.

claim: For some genetic networks high levels of variability in gene expression arise because the properties of the network mean that stochasticity is amplified.
source: One possibility is that for some genetic networks high levels of variability in gene expression arise because the properties of the network mean that stochasticity is amplified.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings of the study.

claim: Genes that were highly variable in their expression between seedlings were enriched for those involved in the response to ABA.
source: Interestingly, the transcriptomic study of Cortijo et al., 2019 showed that genes that were highly variable in their expression between seedlings were enriched for those involved in the response to ABA, supporting the idea that the bistable switch governing ABA levels amplifies stochasticity to generate variability in gene expression and phenotypes.
evidence: This is based on a citation to a published study.

claim: A recent study implicated redundantly acting GA receptors of tomato in maintaining phenotypic stability of plant growth (i.e. low variability) under ambient conditions.
source: In further support of a potential role of the ABA-GA bistable switch in regulating phenotypic variability beyond germination, a recent study implicated redundantly acting GA receptors of tomato in maintaining phenotypic stability of plant growth (i.e. low variability) under ambient conditions (Illouz-Eliaz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a published study.

claim: The level of variability in germination times is an important trait that does not always correlate with the most common measure of germination behaviour, which is percentage germination.
source: In general, our work emphasises that the level of variability in germination times is an important trait that does not always correlate with the most common measure of germination behaviour, which is percentage germination.
evidence: This is based on the findings of the study.

claim: To fully understand the roles of germination regulators, future work should involve characterising their effects on the CV of germination time distributions as well as on traits such as percentage germination and average germination time.
source: Thus, to fully understand the roles of germination regulators, future work should involve characterising their effects on the CV of germination time distributions as well as on traits such as percentage germination and average germination time.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Multiple other aspects of Arabidopsis development have been shown to display phenotypic variability, including both whole plant phenotypes such as growth rate and molecular-level phenotypes such as transcript abundance.
source: Multiple other aspects of Arabidopsis development have been shown to display phenotypic variability, including both whole plant phenotypes such as growth rate and molecular-level phenotypes such as transcript abundance (Hall et al., 2007; Cortijo et al., 2019; Jimenez-Gomez et al., 2011; Joseph et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on citations to published studies.

claim: A common feature across studies and traits is that multiple QTL tend to affect variability of a trait, and while some of them also affect the average trait value, others do not.
source: Similar to our findings, a common feature across studies and traits is that multiple QTL tend to affect variability of a trait, and while some of them also affect the average trait value, others do not.
evidence: This is based on comparison to published studies.

claim: Germination time is a plausible system for studying the genetics of inter-individual variability.
source: By establishing variability in germination time as a robust trait that varies between natural accessions of Arabidopsis, our study reveals that germination time is a plausible system for studying the genetics of inter-individual variability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of the study.
